correctness.rationale: For primitive cycle length at most four, a composite maps directly to a prime and consecutive prime states increase by positive k. Therefore every cycle contains a composite and no adjacent composites; the only possibilities are 1 prime/1 composite, 2 primes/1 composite, 2 primes/2 composites alternating, or 3 primes/1 composite. The return prime p must divide 2k in the 3-cycle case, forcing p=2 and an exact 2-power final composite; the 3-prime 4-cycle forces p|3k, thus p=3 and k+1 a power of three. The alternating 4-cycle has q|(p+k), p|(q+k), and CRT yields k=tpq-p-q; the exact largest-prime-factor conditions are sufficient and necessary. All converse transitions and primitive periods are explicit. verify.py checks the predictions against observed actual dynamics for k<=160, but the infinite classification is the symbolic argument, not enumeration.

originality.rationale: Full primary source inspection of Das (2023) finds a period-spectrum question and finite first-occurrence data, but not universal arithmetic conditions for all 3/4-period cycles. Dubickas (2024) proves boundedness for broader maps and studies the prime-compressed map, which does not determine uncompressed lengths. Two directly relevant public research results bound prime-cycle locations or enumerate loops at specific parameters, neither determines all shifts yielding short periods. Searches for the Fermat-prime and CRT smoothness criteria found no covering statement. Residual risk is an unindexed elementary observation.
residual_risks: Unindexed notes or elementary observations could separately give some or all length-three/four conditions.

value.rationale: Das explicitly asks about attainable periods of a natural arithmetic map. This complete iff classification at all positive shift parameters handles both primitive periods three and four, splits four-cycles into structurally different prime/composite patterns, and explains unexpected ties to Fermat primes, two-prime Frobenius-number shifts and smooth predecessor values. This is more than a finite list or arbitrary slice, while no claim about long periods or infinitude is made.
